topics.title: Measurement, units and systems of units

learn.hook: A cricket pitch is 22 yards, a sprint is 100 m and a fever is 102 °F: every measurement is just a number glued to an agreed unit.
points: Measuring a physical quantity means comparing it with a fixed, internationally accepted reference standard called a unit; the result is a number times a unit (e.g. 5 m).
Base (fundamental) quantities such as length, mass and time are independent; their units are base units.
Derived quantities (speed, force, pressure) are built from base quantities, so their units (m s⁻¹, N = kg m s⁻², Pa) are derived units.
A complete set of base units and derived units is a system of units. Older systems: CGS (centimetre, gram, second), FPS (foot, pound, second) and MKS (metre, kilogram, second).
Different countries using different systems caused confusion, so the world agreed on one system: the SI (Système Internationale d'Unités).

example.q: A car covers 72 km in 1 h. Express its speed in the MKS/SI derived unit.

learn.reallife: ISRO's launch data, Indian Railways' timetables and AIIMS lab reports all use SI units, so a value measured in Sriharikota means the same thing in Paris.

games.title: Match the system to its units of length, mass, time
pairs: MKS-based system with seven base units

quiz.q: Measurement of a physical quantity basically involves
options: Comparing it with an accepted reference standard called a unit
quiz.explain: A measurement compares the quantity with a chosen standard (the unit) and reports how many times the unit it contains.
quiz.mistake: Confuses measuring with writing or estimating a value

quiz.q: Which of the following is a derived quantity?
quiz.explain: Pressure is force per unit area, so it is built from mass, length and time. The others are SI base quantities.
quiz.mistake: Treats every everyday quantity as fundamental

quiz.q: The unit of force, newton, written in base SI units is
quiz.explain: F = ma, so 1 N = 1 kg × 1 m s⁻² = 1 kg m s⁻².
quiz.mistake: Uses the unit of momentum (kg m s⁻¹) or energy instead of force

quiz.q: In the CGS system, the unit of mass is the
quiz.explain: CGS stands for centimetre–gram–second, so mass is measured in grams.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up CGS with MKS

quiz.q: A complete set of base units together with all derived units is called
quiz.explain: Base units plus the derived units built from them form a system of units, such as CGS, FPS, MKS or SI.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a system of units with dimensions

quiz.q: Why was a single international system (SI) adopted?
options: SI does not need any derived units
Different countries used different unit systems, which made exchange of scientific data confusing
SI uses only three base units
Older systems had no unit of length
quiz.explain: Many local systems (CGS, FPS, MKS) existed, so data had to be converted constantly. One agreed system removes that confusion.
quiz.mistake: Thinks SI is simpler because it has fewer base units

quiz.q: A train moves 54 km in 1 hour. Its speed in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.explain: Convert km to m and hours to seconds before dividing.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert hours to seconds

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Velocity is a derived quantity.
Reason (R): Its unit, m s⁻¹, is obtained from the base units of length and time.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Velocity = displacement/time, so its unit is made from the base units metre and second. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a quantity is derived only if it has a special named unit

teach.ask: Gappu says: 'My height is 150. Is that a measurement?' Explain what a measurement really needs, and what base and derived quantities are.
teach.praise: Perfect! A number without a unit is meaningless, and now I know speed is built from length and time.
teach.nudge: But 150 what? Tell me what must go with the number, and what makes a quantity 'derived'.

topics.title: SI base units and their modern definitions

learn.hook: Since 2019, the kilogram is no longer a metal cylinder locked in a vault near Paris. It is fixed by Planck's constant, a number that is the same everywhere in the universe.
points: SI has seven base quantities: length (metre, m), mass (kilogram, kg), time (second, s), electric current (ampere, A), thermodynamic temperature (kelvin, K), amount of substance (mole, mol) and luminous intensity (candela, cd).
Each base unit is now defined by fixing the exact value of a fundamental constant.
Second: caesium-133 hyperfine frequency fixed at 9 192 631 770 Hz. Metre: speed of light in vacuum fixed at 299 792 458 m s⁻¹.
Kilogram: Planck constant h fixed. Ampere: elementary charge e fixed. Kelvin: Boltzmann constant k fixed. Mole: Avogadro constant N_A fixed.
Candela: luminous efficacy of monochromatic light of frequency 540 × 10¹² Hz fixed at 683 lm W⁻¹.

example.q: Which constant fixes the metre, and how far does light travel in 1 s by that definition?
steps: The metre is defined by fixing the speed of light in vacuum, c.
So in 1 s light travels exactly 299 792 458 m.

learn.reallife: The National Physical Laboratory (CSIR-NPL) in New Delhi keeps India's national standards and supplies Indian Standard Time, linked to the caesium definition of the second.

games.title: SI base units: true or false?
items: There are seven SI base units.
m, kg, s, A, K, mol and cd.
The SI unit of temperature is the degree Celsius.
The SI base unit is the kelvin; °C is a derived unit in common use.
The kilogram is now defined using the Planck constant.
Since 2019 h has a fixed exact value that defines the kilogram.
The candela is the SI unit of electric current.
Current is in ampere; candela is for luminous intensity.
The metre is defined by fixing the speed of light in vacuum.
c is fixed at 299 792 458 m s⁻¹.
The mole is the SI unit of mass.
The mole measures amount of substance; mass is in kilograms.

quiz.q: How many base quantities does the SI system have?
quiz.explain: Length, mass, time, electric current, thermodynamic temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity: seven.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the three mechanical quantities (M, L, T)

quiz.q: The SI unit of luminous intensity is the
quiz.explain: Luminous intensity is a base quantity with base unit candela (cd). Lumen and lux are derived units.
quiz.mistake: Confuses luminous intensity with luminous flux or illuminance

quiz.q: Which fundamental constant is fixed to define the kilogram?
quiz.explain: The 2019 redefinition fixes h, and the kilogram follows from it (together with the definitions of the metre and second).
quiz.mistake: Thinks gravity or Avogadro's number defines the kilogram

quiz.q: The second is defined using the radiation of
quiz.explain: The unperturbed ground-state hyperfine transition frequency of caesium-133 is fixed at 9 192 631 770 Hz.
quiz.mistake: Recalls an old (krypton) length standard instead

quiz.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
quiz.explain: The SI base unit of amount of substance is the mole. Temperature is in kelvin, current in ampere and mass in kilogram.
quiz.mistake: Uses everyday or CGS units as SI base units

quiz.q: The ampere is now defined by fixing the value of
options: The permeability of free space only
quiz.explain: e is fixed at 1.602 176 634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and the ampere follows (with the second).
quiz.mistake: Remembers the old 'force between two wires' definition only

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT an SI base unit?
quiz.explain: The newton (kg m s⁻²) is derived from base units; kelvin, mole and candela are base units.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every named unit is a base unit

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The kelvin is defined by fixing the numerical value of the Boltzmann constant.
Reason (R): The kelvin is one of the seven SI base units.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both statements are true, but being a base unit says nothing about how the kelvin is defined; the definition comes from fixing k.
quiz.mistake: Treats any true statement about the kelvin as the reason

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why don't scientists just keep one metal kilogram in a box and compare everything with it?' Explain how SI base units are defined now.
teach.praise: Wow, so every lab on Earth can rebuild the units from constants of nature. No box needed!
teach.nudge: Which special numbers of nature are fixed now? Name at least one and say which unit it defines.

learn.hook: A camera's '24 mm lens', a '4 GB' file and a '5 µm' dust particle all use prefixes. Get them wrong and your answer is off by a factor of a thousand or more!
points: Plane angle dθ = ds/r (arc length/radius); its unit is the radian (rad). A full circle is 2π rad.
Solid angle dΩ = dA/r² (area on a sphere/radius squared); its unit is the steradian (sr). A full sphere subtends 4π sr.
Both are ratios of like quantities, so they are dimensionless.
Prefixes: pico p 10⁻¹², nano n 10⁻⁹, micro µ 10⁻⁶, milli m 10⁻³, centi c 10⁻², kilo k 10³, mega M 10⁶, giga G 10⁹, tera T 10¹².
Symbol rules: unit symbols are not plural and take no full stop (5 kg, not 5 kgs.); units named after people take a capital symbol (N, Pa, K) but are written in lowercase in full (newton).

example.q: An arc of length 0.5 m is cut on a circle of radius 2 m. Find the angle in radians.

learn.reallife: Chip makers quote transistor sizes in nanometres, and a hard disk of 1 TB holds 10¹² bytes. The steradian is used by lighting engineers designing stadium floodlights for IPL night matches.

quiz.q: An arc of length 6 cm subtends an angle at the centre of a circle of radius 3 cm. The angle in radians is
quiz.explain: θ = arc/radius = 6/3 = 2 rad.
quiz.mistake: Divides radius by arc, or multiplies them

quiz.q: A full sphere subtends a solid angle of nπ steradian at its centre. What is n?
quiz.explain: Ω = A/r² = 4πr²/r² = 4π sr.
quiz.mistake: Uses the plane-angle result 2π for a full sphere

quiz.q: The unit of solid angle is the
quiz.explain: Solid angle dΩ = dA/r² is measured in steradians (sr).
quiz.mistake: Confuses solid angle with plane angle

quiz.q: Which prefix stands for 10⁻⁶?
quiz.explain: micro (µ) = 10⁻⁶; milli = 10⁻³; nano = 10⁻⁹; mega = 10⁶.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up micro with milli

quiz.q: Which way of writing a mass follows the SI rules for unit symbols?
options: 25 kg. with a full stop, since it is an abbreviation
25 KG, since symbols are always capitals
25 Kgs, since the mass is more than one kilogram
25 kg, with a lowercase symbol, no plural 's' and no full stop
quiz.explain: The kilogram symbol is lowercase 'kg', is never pluralised, and is not an abbreviation needing a full stop.
quiz.mistake: Pluralises or capitalises unit symbols

quiz.q: A wavelength of 600 nm expressed in metres is 600 × 10⁻ⁿ m. What is n?
quiz.explain: nano means 10⁻⁹, so 600 nm = 600 × 10⁻⁹ m = 6 × 10⁻⁷ m.
quiz.mistake: Uses the micro factor 10⁻⁶ for nano

quiz.q: Why is the radian called a dimensionless unit?
options: It is defined only for small angles
It is a ratio of two areas
It is a ratio of two lengths (arc/radius)
quiz.explain: θ = s/r divides one length by another, so the dimensions cancel.
quiz.mistake: Thinks dimensionless means the quantity has no value

quiz.q: The symbol of the newton is a capital N, but the unit is written 'newton' in full. Which rule explains this?
options: All unit symbols are written in capitals
A capital letter shows that the unit is derived
Symbols of units named after people start with a capital letter; the full name is written in lowercase
Only base units have capital symbols
quiz.explain: Units named after scientists (N, Pa, J, K) get a capital symbol, while the full unit name stays lowercase.
quiz.mistake: Thinks capitals mark base or derived units

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: 'Is a radian a length? And what on earth is a steradian?' Explain both and how prefixes work.
teach.praise: Got it: radian is arc over radius, steradian is area over radius squared, and prefixes are powers of ten!
teach.nudge: What do you divide to get a radian? And what about a steradian? Also tell me what 'kilo' or 'micro' mean.

learn.hook: Astronomers love light years, chemists love ångströms, and physicists love electron volts. The trick is converting cleanly to SI.
points: Litre: 1 L = 10⁻³ m³ = 1000 cm³.
Ångström: 1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m; fermi: 1 fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m (nuclear sizes).
Light year (distance light travels in one year): 1 ly ≈ 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m. Astronomical unit (mean Earth–Sun distance): 1 AU ≈ 1.496 × 10¹¹ m.
Electron volt (energy gained by an electron through 1 V): 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
Convert by replacing each unit with its SI value: 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m², 1 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³, 1 J = 10⁷ erg.

example.q: Convert the density of water, 1 g cm⁻³, into kg m⁻³.

learn.reallife: ISRO's Mars Orbiter Mission distances are often given in AU and km, while a typical Indian household water tank holds 1000 L = 1 m³ of water.

quiz.q: How many cm² are there in 2.5 m²?
quiz.explain: 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m² = 10⁴ cm².
quiz.mistake: Converts area with the length factor 100 instead of 100²

quiz.q: The density of mercury is 13.6 g cm⁻³. In kg m⁻³ it is
quiz.explain: 1 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³, so 13.6 g cm⁻³ = 13600 kg m⁻³.
steps: 1 g cm⁻³ = 10⁻³ kg / 10⁻⁶ m³ = 10³ kg m⁻³
quiz.mistake: Divides by 1000 instead of multiplying

quiz.q: 1 J equals 10ⁿ erg. What is n?
quiz.explain: 1 J = 1 kg m² s⁻² = (10³ g)(10⁴ cm²) s⁻² = 10⁷ g cm² s⁻² = 10⁷ erg.
quiz.mistake: Uses the force factor 10⁵ (newton to dyne)

quiz.q: A 1.5 L bottle has a volume of how many cm³?
quiz.mistake: Treats 1 L as 100 cm³

quiz.q: Which of these is a unit of distance, not of time?
quiz.explain: A light year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'year' in the name makes it a unit of time

quiz.q: Energy of 5 eV in units of 10⁻¹⁹ J is
quiz.explain: 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so 5 eV = 8 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by 1.6

quiz.q: The size of an atom is about 1 Å. How many ångströms make 1 nm?
quiz.explain: 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m and 1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m, so 1 nm = 10 Å.
quiz.mistake: Inverts the ratio

quiz.q: The astronomical unit (AU) is
options: The mean distance between the Earth and the Sun
The distance light travels in one second
The distance between the Sun and the nearest star
quiz.explain: 1 AU ≈ 1.496 × 10¹¹ m is the average Earth–Sun distance.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the AU with the light year or parsec

teach.ask: Gappu read that a star is '4 light years' away and thinks that is a time. Explain non-SI units and how to convert them to SI.
teach.praise: Oh, a light year is a distance! And converting is just swapping each unit with its SI value.
teach.nudge: Is a light year a time or a distance? And how would you change it into metres?

topics.title: Significant figures and the counting rules

learn.hook: Your lab partner writes 2.50 cm and you write 2.5 cm. Same length? Not quite: the extra zero says your partner measured more precisely.
points: Significant figures = all reliably known digits + the first uncertain digit. More significant figures means a more precise measurement.
All non-zero digits are significant; zeros between non-zero digits are significant (2008 has 4).
In a number less than 1, zeros before the first non-zero digit are NOT significant (0.0045 has 2).
Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant (4.500 has 4). In a number without a decimal point, trailing zeros are ambiguous (4500 could have 2, 3 or 4).
The power of ten is never counted: 4.50 × 10³ has 3 significant figures.

example.q: How many significant figures are in (a) 0.007020 (b) 30.040?
steps: (a) Leading zeros 0.00 are not significant. Digits 7, 0, 2, 0 count: the middle zero lies between 7 and 2, the last zero is after the decimal point.
(b) All digits 3, 0, 0, 4, 0 count: zeros in between and the trailing zero after the decimal point.

learn.reallife: AIIMS blood reports print haemoglobin as 13.5 g/dL, not 13.50 or 14, because the analyser's precision fixes the digits that can be trusted.

games.title: Zero rules
items: Leading zeros only locate the decimal point.
In 5.200 the last two zeros are significant.
Trailing zeros after the decimal point are significant.
The number 7300 definitely has 4 significant figures.
Without a decimal point, trailing zeros are ambiguous.
The power of ten in 3.2 × 10⁵ adds to the count of significant figures.
Only the digits 3 and 2 are counted.

quiz.q: The number of significant figures in 0.06900 is
quiz.explain: Leading zeros are not significant. 6, 9 and the two trailing zeros after the decimal point are significant.
quiz.mistake: Counts the leading zeros

quiz.q: How many significant figures does 20.07 have?
quiz.explain: Both zeros lie between non-zero digits (2 and 7), so all four digits count.
quiz.mistake: Ignores zeros between non-zero digits

quiz.q: Which number has exactly three significant figures?
quiz.explain: In 0.000340 the leading zeros do not count; 3, 4 and the trailing zero after the decimal do, giving 3.
quiz.mistake: Counts leading zeros or forgets trailing zeros after a decimal point

quiz.q: Why is it unclear how many significant figures 5600 has?
options: Trailing zeros in a number without a decimal point may only be place holders
It has no decimal digits so it has zero significant figures
quiz.explain: Without a decimal point or scientific notation, we cannot tell whether the trailing zeros were measured.
quiz.mistake: Thinks zeros are never or always significant

quiz.q: The number of significant figures in 6.320 × 10⁻⁴ is
quiz.explain: Only the digits in 6.320 count: 6, 3, 2 and the trailing 0. The power of ten is not counted.
quiz.mistake: Counts the exponent or the zeros of 10⁻⁴

quiz.q: Significant figures in a measured value indicate its
quiz.explain: The number of reliable digits plus one uncertain digit shows how finely the value was measured: its precision.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up precision with accuracy

quiz.q: A metre scale has a least count of 1 mm. A length reading recorded correctly is
quiz.explain: With a 1 mm least count you can read to 0.1 cm, so 12.3 cm shows the reliable digits plus one uncertain digit.
quiz.mistake: Writes more digits than the instrument can measure

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): 0.00250 has three significant figures.
Reason (R): Leading zeros in a number less than one are not significant, but trailing zeros after the decimal point are.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The leading zeros are dropped and 2, 5 and the final 0 are counted. R gives exactly that rule.
quiz.mistake: Counts all zeros or none

teach.ask: Gappu measured a pencil as 12.0 cm and wants to write just 12 cm. Explain what significant figures are and the zero rules.
teach.praise: So that zero in 12.0 is a proud measured digit. I'll keep it!
teach.nudge: Which zeros count and which don't? Tell me about zeros before the first digit and zeros at the end.

topics.title: Scientific notation, order of magnitude and exact numbers

learn.hook: The mass of an electron and the mass of the Sun differ by about 60 powers of ten. Scientific notation lets you write both neatly.
points: Scientific notation: write a number as a × 10ᵇ with 1 ≤ a < 10. All digits of a are significant, so ambiguity about zeros disappears (4.700 × 10³ has 4).
Order of magnitude: if a ≤ 5 the order is b; if a > 5 the order is b + 1 (as in NCERT). The Earth's radius 6.4 × 10⁶ m has order 7.
Changing units does not change the number of significant figures: 2.308 cm = 0.02308 m = 23.08 mm, all with 4.
Exact numbers (counted items, or pure numbers like 2 in 2πr, ½ in ½mv²) have unlimited significant figures and never limit a result.

example.q: Write 0.0004070 m in scientific notation and state its significant figures and order of magnitude.
steps: a = 4.070 ≤ 5, so the order of magnitude is −4.

learn.reallife: Indian census figures (about 1.4 × 10⁹ people) and India's GDP in rupees are easiest to compare when written as powers of ten.

games.title: Smallest to largest order of magnitude
Notation facts
items: 4.0 × 10² and 400 always show the same precision.
4.0 × 10² clearly has 2 significant figures; 400 is ambiguous.
Changing 2.308 cm to 0.02308 m keeps 4 significant figures.
Changing units only moves the decimal point; the new leading zeros do not count.
The 2 in the formula 2πr limits the significant figures of the result to one.
It is an exact number with unlimited significant figures.
In 7.5 × 10⁴ the order of magnitude is 5 (NCERT rule).

quiz.q: The radius of a hydrogen atom is about 0.53 Å = 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m. By the NCERT rule its order of magnitude (power of ten) is
quiz.explain: a = 5.3 > 5, so we round up: order = −11 + 1 = −10.
quiz.mistake: Uses the exponent directly without checking whether a > 5

quiz.q: The order of magnitude of 3.2 × 10⁵ m is
quiz.explain: a = 3.2 ≤ 5, so the order is the exponent itself, 5.
quiz.mistake: Always adds one to the exponent

quiz.q: The length 2.540 cm is expressed as 0.02540 m. The number of significant figures is now
quiz.explain: Changing units only shifts the decimal point; the leading zeros added are not significant. Still 4.
quiz.mistake: Counts the new leading zeros

quiz.q: In the expression for kinetic energy ½mv², the number ½ has
quiz.explain: ½ is an exact pure number, so it never limits the precision of the result.
quiz.mistake: Treats an exact constant like a measured value

quiz.q: Which form correctly shows that 3800 m was measured to 3 significant figures?
quiz.explain: 3.80 × 10³ has exactly three significant digits and uses 1 ≤ a < 10.
quiz.mistake: Drops the significant trailing zero or uses non-standard form

quiz.q: A student counted 25 oscillations of a pendulum. The number 25 has
options: Unlimited significant figures since it is an exact count
quiz.explain: Counted numbers are exact; they do not limit the significant figures of a calculation.
quiz.mistake: Treats a count like a measured reading

quiz.q: The mass of the Earth is 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg. Its order of magnitude by the NCERT rule is
quiz.mistake: Ignores the round-up rule

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The number 4500, written without a decimal point, definitely has four significant figures.
Reason (R): Trailing zeros in a number without a decimal point are ambiguous.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: the trailing zeros may only be place holders, so 4500 could have 2, 3 or 4 significant figures. R is true.
quiz.mistake: Counts every trailing zero as significant

teach.ask: Gappu writes the Earth's radius as 6400000 m and can't tell how precise it is. Explain scientific notation, order of magnitude and exact numbers.
teach.praise: 6.4 × 10⁶ m looks so much tidier, and now I know its order is 7. Thanks!
teach.nudge: How would you write it with a power of ten? And what is special about numbers like the 2 in 2πr?

learn.hook: Your calculator says the density is 8.571428571 g cm⁻³. Your ruler was never that good. Significant-figure rules tell you how much of that to keep.
points: Multiplication or division: keep as many significant figures as the factor with the FEWEST significant figures.
Addition or subtraction: keep as many decimal places as the term with the FEWEST decimal places.
Example: 4.237 g ÷ 2.51 cm³ = 1.688… → 1.69 g cm⁻³ (3 sig figs, like 2.51).
Exact numbers (like 4/3 in the sphere volume) do not limit the result.

example.q: A rectangle measures 4.234 m by 1.005 m. Report its area with correct significant figures.

learn.reallife: Pharmacists at Jan Aushadhi Kendras weigh doses carefully: a total can never be reported more precisely than the least precise weighing in it.

quiz.q: The result of 3.0 × 4.123, with correct significant figures, is
quiz.explain: 3.0 has 2 significant figures, so the product (12.369) is rounded to 2: 12.
quiz.mistake: Keeps all the digits from the calculator

quiz.q: 2.5 m + 0.236 m + 1.03 m, reported correctly, is
quiz.explain: The sum is 3.766 m. The least number of decimal places is 1 (in 2.5), so we round to 3.8 m.
quiz.mistake: Uses significant figures instead of decimal places for addition

quiz.q: A mass of 5.74 g occupies 1.2 cm³. Its density in g cm⁻³, correctly reported, is
quiz.explain: 5.74/1.2 = 4.783…; 1.2 has 2 significant figures, so the result is 4.8.
quiz.mistake: Reports as many digits as the more precise value

quiz.q: The side of a cube is 1.2 cm. Its volume, with correct significant figures, in cm³ is
quiz.explain: 1.2³ = 1.728 cm³; the side has 2 significant figures, so V = 1.7 cm³.
quiz.mistake: Thinks cubing a number keeps all calculator digits

quiz.q: Subtract: 12.4 s − 3.25 s. Correctly reported, the result (in s) is
quiz.explain: 12.4 − 3.25 = 9.15 s. Keep 1 decimal place (as in 12.4). The dropped digit is 5 and the preceding 1 is odd, so 9.15 becomes 9.2.
quiz.mistake: Applies the significant-figure count rule to subtraction

quiz.q: For the volume of a sphere V = (4/3)πr³ with r = 2.0 cm, how many significant figures should V have?
quiz.explain: 4/3 and π are exact or can be taken to any precision; r has 2 significant figures, so V has 2.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 4/3 or 3 limits the result to one significant figure

quiz.q: A student finds the area of a sheet 2.1 m × 3.5 m as 7.35 m². The best criticism is
options: The answer should be 7.4 m² because each length has only 2 significant figures
quiz.explain: Product of two 2-significant-figure values must be given to 2 significant figures: 7.35 → 7.4 m².
quiz.mistake: Keeps extra digits from multiplication

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): 436.32 g + 227.2 g + 0.301 g should be reported as 663.8 g.
Reason (R): In addition, the result keeps as many decimal places as the term with the fewest decimal places.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: 227.2 has one decimal place, so the exact sum 663.821 g is reported as 663.8 g. R gives the rule.
quiz.mistake: Applies the multiplication rule to addition

teach.ask: Gappu divided 5.74 g by 1.2 cm³ and proudly wrote 4.783333 g/cm³. Explain how many digits he should keep, for multiplying and for adding.
teach.praise: So 4.8 g/cm³ it is! Multiplying watches significant figures, adding watches decimal places.
teach.nudge: What do you look at when you multiply or divide? And is it the same when you add or subtract?

topics.title: Rounding off and uncertainty in results

learn.hook: Should 2.745 round to 2.74 or 2.75? Physics has a clever tie-breaking rule that avoids always rounding up.
points: If the digit dropped is more than 5, add 1 to the preceding digit; if less than 5, leave it unchanged.
If the digit dropped is exactly 5 (nothing or only zeros after it): leave the preceding digit unchanged if it is even, add 1 if it is odd. So 2.745 → 2.74 and 2.735 → 2.74.
Relative error = Δx/x. For a product or quotient, relative errors add: ΔA/A = Δl/l + Δb/b for A = l × b.
In multi-step calculations, carry one extra digit in intermediate results and round only the final answer.

example.q: A rectangle has l = 16.2 ± 0.1 cm and b = 10.1 ± 0.1 cm. Estimate the percentage error in its area.
steps: Errors add for a product: about 0.6% + 1% ≈ 1.6%.
Area = 163.62 cm², reported as about 164 ± 3 cm².

learn.reallife: Weather stations of the IMD round rainfall readings consistently, so monthly monsoon totals are not biased upward by always rounding 5s up.

games.title: Errors and rounding
items: For A = l × b, the relative error in A is the sum of the relative errors in l and b.
Relative errors add for products and quotients.
You should round every intermediate step to the final number of significant figures.
Carry one extra digit and round at the end.
The dropped digit is 5 and the preceding 3 is odd, so it becomes 4.
The preceding 2 is even, so it stays: 1.22.
A relative error has the same unit as the quantity.
It is a ratio, so it has no unit.

quiz.q: Rounded to three significant figures, 4.0635 becomes
quiz.explain: Keep 4.06; the dropped digits 35 are less than 50, so the 6 is unchanged.
quiz.mistake: Rounds up because a 5 appears somewhere

quiz.q: Following the NCERT rule, 6.375 rounded to three significant figures is
quiz.explain: The dropped digit is exactly 5 and the preceding digit 7 is odd, so it is raised to 8.
quiz.mistake: Leaves an odd preceding digit unchanged

quiz.q: Following the NCERT rule, 3.465 rounded to three significant figures is
quiz.explain: The dropped digit is exactly 5 and the preceding digit 6 is even, so it stays: 3.46.
quiz.mistake: Always rounds 5 upward

quiz.q: Length l = 20.0 ± 0.2 cm. Its percentage error is
quiz.explain: Percentage error = (0.2/20.0) × 100 = 1%.
quiz.mistake: Reports the absolute error as a percentage

quiz.q: For A = l × b with 2% error in l and 3% error in b, the percentage error in A is
quiz.explain: For a product, percentage errors add: 2% + 3% = 5%.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies or subtracts percentage errors

quiz.q: Why should intermediate results carry one extra digit?
options: Because the final answer needs more digits
To avoid building up rounding errors before the final answer
To increase the precision of the measuring instrument
quiz.explain: Rounding at every step adds small errors that pile up. Keep one extra digit and round only at the end.
quiz.mistake: Thinks extra digits make the measurement more precise

quiz.q: The side of a square is measured with 1% error. The percentage error in its area is
quiz.explain: A = a × a, so the relative error is 1% + 1% = 2%.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that both factors carry the same error

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): 2.745 rounded to three significant figures is 2.74.
Reason (R): When the digit dropped is exactly 5, the preceding digit is left unchanged if it is even.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The preceding digit 4 is even, so it stays: 2.74. R states the rule used.
quiz.mistake: Always rounds a 5 upward

teach.ask: Gappu always rounds every 5 up, and rounds at every step of a long sum. Explain the better rules and how errors combine in A = l × b.
teach.praise: Even stays, odd goes up, errors add for products, and I round only at the end. Neat!
teach.nudge: What happens to a dropped 5 when the digit before it is even? And how do errors combine when you multiply?

learn.hook: Kilometres or miles, the 'nature' of a distance is still length. Dimensions capture that nature, ignoring numbers and units.
points: Dimensions of a quantity are the powers to which base quantities must be raised to represent it.
Base dimensions are written in square brackets: [M] mass, [L] length, [T] time, [A] electric current, [K] temperature, [cd] luminous intensity, [mol] amount of substance.
Volume = [L³], velocity = [L T⁻¹], acceleration = [L T⁻²], force = [M L T⁻²].
Dimensions do not depend on the numerical value or the unit: 5 km and 3 miles both have dimension [L].
In mechanics everything can be written using only [M], [L] and [T].

example.q: Find the dimensions of acceleration starting from a = Δv/Δt.
steps: = [L T⁻²], i.e. dimension 1 in length and −2 in time.

learn.reallife: Whether Indian Railways quotes speed in km/h or ISRO quotes it in m/s, the dimension is the same, [L T⁻¹], which lets engineers compare them safely.

games.title: Dimension facts
items: Dimensions depend on the unit used.
The nature of a quantity is the same in any unit.
Force has dimension 1 in mass, 1 in length and −2 in time.
[K] is the symbol for the dimension of electric current.
Speed and velocity have the same dimensions.

quiz.q: The dimensions of velocity are
quiz.explain: Velocity = displacement/time = [L]/[T] = [L T⁻¹], with no mass dependence.
quiz.mistake: Includes mass or uses the acceleration exponent

quiz.q: Force has dimension in time equal to
quiz.explain: [F] = [M L T⁻²], so the power of T is −2.
quiz.mistake: Drops the sign of the exponent

quiz.q: Which of these quantities has dimensions [L³]?
quiz.explain: Volume is length × length × length = [L³].
quiz.mistake: Confuses area [L²] with volume

quiz.q: The symbol for the dimension of thermodynamic temperature is
quiz.explain: NCERT uses [K] for temperature; [T] is time and [A] is current.
quiz.mistake: Uses [T] for temperature

quiz.q: The power of [L] in the dimensions of acceleration is
quiz.explain: [a] = [L T⁻²]: power 1 for length, −2 for time.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the powers of L and T

quiz.q: A distance of 5 km and a distance of 5000 m have
quiz.explain: Dimensions describe the nature of a quantity, not its unit or size.
quiz.mistake: Thinks changing units changes dimensions

quiz.q: Which pair has the same dimensions?
quiz.explain: Speed and velocity are both [L T⁻¹]. Force [M L T⁻²] ≠ momentum [M L T⁻¹]; weight is a force.
quiz.mistake: Treats mass and weight as the same quantity

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Dimensions of a physical quantity do not change when it is expressed in a different system of units.
Reason (R): Dimensions show the nature of a quantity in terms of base quantities, not its unit.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A length is [L] in cm, m or feet. R explains why.
quiz.mistake: Confuses units with dimensions

teach.ask: Gappu thinks 'dimensions' only means length, breadth and height. Explain what dimensions mean in physics with an example.
teach.praise: So force is [M L T⁻²], whatever unit I use. Physics dimensions are about nature, not boxes!
teach.nudge: What do the powers in [L T⁻¹] tell you? And do dimensions change if you change units?

learn.hook: Work, energy and torque all share the same dimensional formula. Pressure and stress do too. Spotting twins like these is a favourite exam trick.
points: Dimensional formula: shows which base quantities, with which powers, make up a quantity, e.g. velocity [M⁰ L T⁻¹].
Dimensional equation: equating a quantity to its formula, e.g. [F] = [M L T⁻²].
From definitions: work/energy = F × d → [M L² T⁻²]; power = W/t → [M L² T⁻³]; pressure = F/A → [M L⁻¹ T⁻²]; momentum = mv → [M L T⁻¹]; density = m/V → [M L⁻³].
Dimensionless quantities (ratios of like quantities): angle, strain, refractive index, relative density. Their dimensional formula is [M⁰ L⁰ T⁰].

example.q: Derive the dimensional formula of pressure.

learn.reallife: Water-supply engineers in Indian cities quote pipe pressure in pascals and pump power in watts; checking dimensions keeps those design sheets error-free.

quiz.q: The dimensional formula of work is
quiz.explain: Work = force × displacement = [M L T⁻²][L] = [M L² T⁻²].
quiz.mistake: Gives the formula of force or power instead

quiz.q: The dimensional formula of power is
quiz.explain: Power = work/time = [M L² T⁻²]/[T] = [M L² T⁻³].
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by time

quiz.q: Which physical quantity has the same dimensions as pressure?
quiz.explain: Stress = force/area, just like pressure, so both are [M L⁻¹ T⁻²].
quiz.mistake: Picks strain, which is dimensionless

quiz.q: Momentum has the dimensional formula
quiz.explain: p = mv = [M][L T⁻¹] = [M L T⁻¹].
quiz.mistake: Confuses momentum with force

quiz.q: Which of these is dimensionless?
quiz.explain: Refractive index = speed of light in vacuum/speed in medium, a ratio of like quantities.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every quantity with a special name has dimensions

quiz.q: What is the power of [L] in the dimensional formula of density?
quiz.explain: ρ = m/V = [M]/[L³] = [M L⁻³].
quiz.mistake: Forgets that volume is in the denominator

quiz.q: The dimensional equation for force is written as
quiz.explain: A dimensional equation sets the quantity in brackets equal to its dimensional formula.
quiz.mistake: Writes dimensions without brackets or adds powers

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Relative density is a dimensionless quantity.
Reason (R): Relative density has the SI unit kg m⁻³.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true: it is a ratio of two densities. R is false: being a ratio, it has no unit.
quiz.mistake: Confuses relative density with density

teach.ask: Gappu wants a shortcut to find the dimensional formula of any quantity, like pressure or power. Teach him the method and name some dimensionless quantities.
teach.praise: Start from the definition and replace each quantity by its dimensions. Easy-peasy!
teach.nudge: What do you start from to build a dimensional formula? And which quantities end up with no dimensions at all?

topics.title: Principle of homogeneity and checking equations

learn.hook: You can't add 5 kg to 3 m, just like you can't add rupees to kilometres. That simple idea catches wrong formulas instantly.
points: Principle of homogeneity: only quantities with the same dimensions can be added, subtracted or equated.
So every term on both sides of a correct equation has the same dimensions.
Arguments of sin, cos, exponential and log functions must be dimensionless (e.g. ωt in sin ωt).
Check x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at²: [L], [L T⁻¹][T] = [L], [L T⁻²][T²] = [L]. All terms are [L], so it is consistent.
A dimensionally consistent equation may still be wrong (e.g. a missing ½), but a dimensionally inconsistent one is certainly wrong.

example.q: Check whether v² = u² + 2as is dimensionally consistent.
steps: All terms match, so the equation is dimensionally consistent.

learn.reallife: Before simulations of a monsoon model run on IITM Pune's supercomputer, scientists check each equation term by term, exactly like this.

games.title: Homogeneity facts
items: A dimensionally correct equation is always physically correct.
Dimensionless factors like ½ or 2π cannot be checked.
A dimensionally wrong equation is definitely wrong.
Terms with different dimensions cannot be equated.
In y = A sin(ωt), the product ωt must be dimensionless.
Arguments of trigonometric functions are dimensionless.
You may add a force to a momentum if both are vectors.
Both sides of a correct equation must have the same dimensions.
This is the principle of homogeneity.

quiz.q: According to the principle of homogeneity, two quantities can be added only if they
options: Are measured with the same instrument
quiz.explain: Addition and subtraction make sense only for like quantities, i.e. same dimensions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks being vectors is enough

quiz.q: Which equation is dimensionally incorrect? (s distance, u, v velocities, a acceleration, t time)
quiz.explain: [at³] = [L T⁻²][T³] = [L T], not [L], so s = ut + at³ fails.
quiz.mistake: Checks only one term of the equation

quiz.q: In y = A sin(kx − ωt), where x is a length, the dimensions of k are
quiz.explain: kx must be dimensionless, so [k] = 1/[L] = [L⁻¹].
quiz.mistake: Forgets that a trigonometric argument must be dimensionless

quiz.q: In y = A sin(kx − ωt), the dimensions of ω are
quiz.explain: ωt is dimensionless, so [ω] = [T⁻¹].
quiz.mistake: Mixes up ω with k

quiz.q: x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² passes the dimensional test. This proves that
options: The equation is certainly correct, including the ½
Each term has dimensions of length, but the factor ½ is not confirmed
quiz.explain: Dimensional analysis shows consistency only; it cannot check dimensionless factors like ½.
quiz.mistake: Believes a dimensional check proves an equation completely

quiz.q: A student writes the formula for the period of a pendulum as T = 2π√(g/l). Using dimensions, this is
quiz.explain: [g/l] = [L T⁻²]/[L] = [T⁻²], so √(g/l) = [T⁻¹], not [T]. The correct formula is T = 2π√(l/g).
quiz.mistake: Thinks 2π carries dimensions

quiz.q: In the expression e^(−αt), where t is time, the dimension of α is
quiz.explain: The exponent αt must be dimensionless, so [α] = [T⁻¹].
quiz.mistake: Thinks only trigonometric arguments must be dimensionless

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A dimensionally correct equation may not be a correct physical relation.
Reason (R): Dimensionless constants such as ½ or 2π cannot be found or checked by dimensional analysis.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because pure numbers carry no dimensions, an equation with a wrong numerical factor still passes. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks dimensional analysis checks everything

teach.ask: Gappu wrote s = ut + at³ and wants to know if it can be right. Explain the principle of homogeneity and what a dimensional check can and cannot prove.
teach.praise: Every term must match, sine's argument must have no dimensions, and passing the test doesn't guarantee correctness. Got it!
teach.nudge: Do all terms in a correct equation need the same dimensions? And does passing the check prove the formula?

topics.title: Testing formulae and finding dimensions of constants

learn.hook: In CBSE papers you are often given 'v = at + b/(t + c)' and asked for the dimensions of a, b and c. It is a quick 2–3 mark win once you see the trick.
points: To test an energy relation, compare dimensions: ½mv² → [M][L T⁻¹]² = [M L² T⁻²]; mgh → [M][L T⁻²][L] = [M L² T⁻²]. Both match energy.
To find a constant, make each added term match the left side, and quantities added together must have the same dimensions.
Example: v = at + b/(t + c). [c] = [T] (added to t); [at] = [v] → [a] = [L T⁻²]; [b/T] = [v] → [b] = [L].
To spot the wrong formula among several, check each term; any mismatch rules it out.

example.q: In P = a/b + x/(b + t²), with P a pressure and t a time, find the dimensions of b.
steps: b is added to t², so [b] = [t²] = [T²].
That is enough for b; a and x can be found similarly.

learn.reallife: Engineers at BHEL quickly verify vendor formulas for turbine power by dimensions before using them in design.

games.title: v = at + b/(t + c): constant ↔ dimensions

quiz.q: Which expression has the dimensions of energy?
quiz.explain: [m][g][h] = [M][L T⁻²][L] = [M L² T⁻²], the dimensions of energy.
quiz.mistake: Confuses energy with momentum or force

quiz.q: In v = at + b/(t + c), the dimensions of c are
quiz.explain: c is added to t, so it must have the dimensions of time.
quiz.mistake: Thinks c must match v

quiz.q: In v = at + b/(t + c), the dimensions of b are
quiz.explain: b/(t + c) must be a velocity, so [b] = [L T⁻¹][T] = [L].
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by the time in the denominator

quiz.q: In v = at + b/(t + c), the dimensions of a are
quiz.explain: at must be a velocity, so [a] = [L T⁻¹]/[T] = [L T⁻²].
quiz.mistake: Gives a the dimensions of velocity

quiz.q: Which formula for the kinetic energy K of a body of mass m and speed v could be correct on dimensional grounds?
quiz.explain: m²v³/(2mv) simplifies to mv²/2, which is [M L² T⁻²]. The others give [M L T⁻¹], [M² L² T⁻²] or [M L³ T⁻³].
quiz.mistake: Does not simplify the expression before checking

quiz.q: In the van der Waals form (P + a/V²)(V − b) = RT, the dimensions of b are those of
quiz.explain: b is subtracted from V, so it has the dimensions of volume, [L³].
quiz.mistake: Thinks b must match P

quiz.q: In (P + a/V²)(V − b) = RT, the constant a has the dimensions of
quiz.explain: a/V² is added to P, so [a] = [P][V²] = [M L⁻¹ T⁻²][L⁶] = [M L⁵ T⁻²].
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply back by V²

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Both ½mv² and mgh are dimensionally correct expressions for energy.
Reason (R): Each has dimensions [M L² T⁻²].
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: [M][L T⁻¹]² and [M][L T⁻²][L] both give [M L² T⁻²]. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ½ changes the dimensions

teach.ask: Gappu found the formula v = at + b/(t + c) and has no idea what a, b and c are. Teach him how to find their dimensions.
teach.praise: Whatever is added to t must be time, and every term must be a velocity. I can crack these now!
teach.nudge: What must c be if it is added to t? And what must each term on the right be equal to?

topics.title: Deducing relations by dimensional analysis and its limits

learn.hook: Without any calculus, you can predict that a pendulum twice as long ticks √2 times slower. Dimensional analysis is that powerful.
points: Assume the quantity depends on the others as a power law, e.g. T = k lᵃ gᵇ mᶜ, and equate powers of M, L and T on both sides.
Pendulum: [T] = [L]ᵃ [L T⁻²]ᵇ [M]ᶜ → c = 0, a + b = 0, −2b = 1 → b = −½, a = ½. So T = k√(l/g) (k = 2π from theory).
Unit conversion: n₂ = n₁[M₁/M₂]ᵃ[L₁/L₂]ᵇ[T₁/T₂]ᶜ for a quantity of dimensions [Mᵃ Lᵇ Tᶜ]. E.g. 1 N = 10⁵ dyne.

Limitations: dimensionless constants (like 2π) cannot be found; it fails for relations with sums/differences of terms or trigonometric/exponential functions, and when a quantity depends on more than three variables in mechanics (only three equations: M, L, T).

example.q: Convert 1 J into erg using dimensions.
steps: [Energy] = [M L² T⁻²], so a = 1, b = 2, c = −2.
M₁ = 1 kg = 10³ g, L₁ = 1 m = 10² cm, T₁ = T₂ = 1 s.

learn.reallife: Before building costly wind tunnels, aerospace engineers at NAL Bengaluru use dimensional analysis to predict how forces scale with speed and size.

games.title: Steps to get the pendulum formula
items: Write dimensions of each side: [T] = [L]ᵃ[L T⁻²]ᵇ[M]ᶜ
Equate powers of M, L and T

games.title: Limits of dimensional analysis
items: It can find the value 2π in T = 2π√(l/g).
It cannot derive a relation like s = ut + ½at² that has a sum of terms.
Power-law assumption gives only one term.
In mechanics it can handle a dependence on at most three quantities.
Only three equations (for M, L, T) are available.
It shows that a pendulum's period is independent of the bob's mass.
The power of mass comes out zero.
It can derive y = A sin ωt.

quiz.q: By dimensional analysis, the time period of a simple pendulum is proportional to l raised to the power
quiz.explain: Equating powers gives a = ½ and b = −½, so T ∝ √(l/g).
quiz.mistake: Solves the exponent equations with a sign slip

quiz.q: Using dimensions, 1 N equals 10ⁿ dyne. What is n?
quiz.mistake: Uses the energy conversion 10⁷

quiz.q: A pendulum's length is made 4 times larger. Its period becomes how many times the original?
quiz.explain: T ∝ √l, so the period becomes √4 = 2 times.
quiz.mistake: Assumes T ∝ l

quiz.q: Which of these can dimensional analysis NOT do?
options: Find how one quantity depends on others in a simple power law
Check the consistency of an equation
Find the value of a dimensionless constant like 2π
quiz.explain: Pure numbers have no dimensions, so their values cannot be obtained.
quiz.mistake: Thinks dimensional analysis gives complete formulas

quiz.q: The speed v of a wave on a string depends on tension F [M L T⁻²] and mass per unit length μ [M L⁻¹]. Dimensional analysis gives v ∝
quiz.explain: Fᵃμᵇ: M: a + b = 0; L: a − b = 1; T: −2a = −1 → a = ½, b = −½. So v ∝ √(F/μ).
quiz.mistake: Inverts the ratio

quiz.q: Pressure is 10⁵ Pa. In CGS units (dyne cm⁻²) this is 10ⁿ. What is n?
quiz.explain: [P] = [M L⁻¹ T⁻²]: n₂ = n₁ (10³)¹(10²)⁻¹ = 10 n₁. So 10⁵ Pa = 10⁶ dyne cm⁻².
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the length power is −1

quiz.q: Why can dimensional analysis not derive a relation in which a quantity depends on four variables in mechanics?
options: There are only three equations (from M, L and T) to fix four unknown powers
quiz.explain: Matching powers of M, L and T gives only three equations, which cannot fix four exponents.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the problem is the constant only

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Dimensional analysis can give the value of the constant 2π in T = 2π√(l/g).
Reason (R): Dimensional analysis works by equating the powers of M, L and T on both sides of a relation.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: pure numbers like 2π have no dimensions, so they cannot be found. R correctly describes the method.
quiz.mistake: Thinks dimensional analysis gives complete formulas

teach.ask: Gappu wants to guess how a pendulum's period depends on its length without any experiments. Show him the dimensional method and warn him about its limits.
teach.praise: Assume a power law, match M, L and T, and remember it can't find 2π. That's a magic trick with rules!
teach.nudge: How do you begin, and what do you compare on both sides? Also, is there anything the method can't tell you?
